By the wise Dattatreya, the boon-giver, a boon was given to the wise Kartavirya, king of the Haihayas:

These two arms of yours, king, for my sake will become a thousand arms, no doubt.
brahmapuran:213:112	You will protect the whole earth, lord of the earth, and be hard for hosts of enemies to look at when you stand in battle.
This is your glorious, wondrous, auspicious Vaishnava manifestation. Again there is this manifestation of the great-souled Jamadagni's son,
in which Rama, the lord, killed King Arjuna, hard to conquer in battle by foes, who had a thousand arms, standing in his army.
Rama felled the king Arjuna on the earth as he stood in his chariot, and having overpowered Arjuna who roared like a cloud,
the Bhrigu's delight cut off all his thousand arms with his blazing axe, together with his kinsmen.
The earth, adorned with Meru and Mandara, filled with ten million Kshatriyas, was made free of Kshatriyas by him twenty-one times.
Having made her free of Kshatriyas, the greatly famed Bhargava performed the horse-sacrifice for the destruction of all sin.
In that sacrifice of great giving, the Bhrigu's delight, pleased, gave the earth as fee to Marichi's son Kashyapa.
Elephants, white horses and chariots, the best of charioteers, imperishable gold, cows and king-elephants the king gave
in that great horse-sacrifice, greatly famed; and even today, for the good of the worlds, the Bhrigu's delight,
practising fierce austerity, the lord Jamadagni's son again lives, glorious, like a god on the best of mountains, Mahendra.
This manifestation of the great-souled Vishnu, lord of gods, eternal and imperishable, is famed as Jamadagnya.
In the twenty-fourth yuga, with Vishvamitra in front, was born a son of Dasharatha, lotus-eyed.
The mighty-armed lord, dividing himself fourfold, was famed in the world as Rama, like the sun in brilliance.
For the pleasure of the world, the subjugation of Rakshasas and the growth of dharma, the greatly famed one was born there.
They call him the king of men, devoted to the welfare of all beings, who knew all dharma and lived in the forest fourteen years.
Rama, with Lakshmana as follower, devoted to the welfare of all beings, practised austerity in the forest for fourteen years, the Raghava.
Beside him stood in form the one famed among people as Sita, who is the Lakshmi mentioned before, following her husband.
Living in Janasthana he did the work of the gods; the best of men, to the cruel descendant of Pulastya who wronged him,
seeking Sita's trace, the greatly famed one killed (Rakshasas); of the gods and Asuras, Yakshas, Rakshasas and serpents,
in which battle he killed Ravana, the Rakshasa-king unslayable, hard to conquer, attended by ten million Rakshasas, like a heap of dark collyrium,
the cruel Ravana, lord of Rakshasas, the terror of the three worlds, hard to conquer, hard to withstand, proud, with the valour of a tiger,
hard for the hosts of gods to look at, proud of his boon: he killed Ravana in battle together with his ministers and army.
Resembling a mass of great clouds, huge-bodied, very strong, Ravana was quickly killed by Rama, lord of beings, formerly,
by whom, for Sugriva's sake, the monkey-lord, mighty Vali, was slain in battle, and Sugriva was consecrated;
and the proud son of Madhu, the Danava named Lavana, was killed in Madhuvana, the hero and great Asura, intoxicated with a boon;
by whom Maricha and Subahu, the best of the strong, who obstructed the sacrifice of the purified-souled sages,
were killed and made hopeless in battle by that great-souled one, skilled in fighting, and other Rakshasas too.
Viradha and Kabandha, the two Rakshasas of terrible valour, deluded by a curse as Gandharvas, the tiger among men killed.
With arrows resembling fire, sun-rays and lightning in splendour, with golden-glittering varied feathers, of strength like Indra's thunderbolt, Rama killed his enemies in battle.
Weapons were given to him by the wise Vishvamitra for the killing of the gods' enemies, unassailable even by gods.
By him, at the sacrifice in progress of the great-souled Janaka, Shiva's bow was broken in sport formerly.
Having done these deeds, Rama, best of the upholders of dharma, performed ten horse-sacrifices with Jaruthya, unrestrained.
No inauspicious words were heard, the wind did not blow harmfully, and there was no theft of wealth when Rama ruled the kingdom.
Widows lamented not, and misfortune never came; all was auspicious there when Rama ruled the kingdom.
There was no fear for beings from water, fire or wind, nor did old people perform funeral rites for the young.
The Kshatriyas were devoted to celibacy, the Vaishyas devoted to the Kshatriyas, and the Shudras served the three varnas without egoism.
Women did not wrong husbands, and the husband did not wrong his wife; the whole world was self-controlled and the earth was without robbers.
Rama alone was the husband, Rama the protector; there were thousands of years and people with thousands of sons.
Creatures were free of disease when Rama ruled the kingdom; of gods, sages and humans there was in all ways
a gathering on earth when Rama ruled the kingdom. Here those people who know the Puranas sing a verse,
bound to the truth in Rama, of his wise greatness: dark, young, red-eyed, bright-faced, of measured speech,
long-armed, fair-faced, lion-shouldered, mighty-armed, Rama ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
The sound of the Rik, Sama and Yajus and the sound of the great-souled one's bowstring were unbroken in the kingdom, with "Give and eat."
Full of sattva, endowed with virtues, shining with his own brilliance, Rama, Dasharatha's son, outshone moon and sun.
He sacrificed with a hundred holy sacrifices with the prescribed boons and fees, and the mighty Raghava, leaving Ayodhya, went to heaven.
Thus the mighty-armed one, delight of the Ikshvaku family, having killed Ravana with his host, went to heaven, the lord.
Another manifestation of Keshava, the great-souled one, is famed in the Mathura kalpa for the welfare of all worlds,
in which he, the valiant, with a human body slew Shalva, Chaidya, Kamsa, Dvivida, Arishta, Vrishabha, Keshi, and the Daitya woman Putana,
the elephant Kuvalayapida, Chanura and Mushtika, and Daityas;
Bana's thousand arms of wondrous deeds were cut off, and Naraka and the mighty Yavana were killed in battle,
and all the jewels of kings were taken by his brilliance, and the kings on earth of evil conduct were laid low.
This manifestation of the great-souled one for the world's welfare is Kalki, named Vishnuyashas, born in the village of Shambhala,
again the god of great fame for the welfare of all worlds. These and many others, divine, surrounded by hosts of gods,
manifestations are sung in the Puranas by the speakers of Brahman, in the recital of which manifestations the gods are bewildered.
Where the Purana, consisting of Vedic heard tradition, is — by mere indication here, the recital of manifestations
of the praiseworthy lord, teacher of all worlds, has been told; by reciting the manifestations his ancestors are pleased.
He who with joined palms hears of Vishnu of immeasurable valour —
hearing these maya-yogas of the Lord of yogis a man is freed from all sins and quickly obtains prosperity, abundance and vast enjoyments by the Lord's grace.
Thus, best of sages, the holy manifestations of Vishnu of immeasurable brilliance, removers of all sin, have been told by me.
One who does not abandon dharma out of desire, anger or hatred, who acts as said, and is gentle, meets a happy death.
Men who give water to the thirsty and food to the hungry meet in time a death joined with happiness.
Givers of wealth conquer cold, givers of sandal conquer heat, and those who bear another's anxiety conquer painful, life-destroying pain.
Givers of knowledge conquer delusion, and givers of lamps darkness; a false witness, a liar, and a teacher who does not instruct —
all these meet the death of delusion, and so do reviLers of the Veda. Terrifying, foul-smelling, with deceitful clubs in hand,
the evil-souled servants of Yama come; when they come within sight, trembling arises in him.
He cries out incessantly for his brother, mother and father; that speech, Brahmins, is indistinct and appears of one syllable.
His sight whirls from fear, his mouth is parched by cough; then, seized by pain, he leaves that body.
Following the wind's front, he takes another body of that form, for the torment of his actions, not born of mother and father.
By the measure of age, stage and constitution of that body he suffers pain; then Yama's messenger binds him with terrible nooses.
Of a creature whose time has come, greatly afflicted with pain, his body abandoned by the elements, his breath reaching the throat,
the soul, made to leave the body, cries loudly; gone out as wind, in a body of six sheaths,
he is abandoned on earth by mothers, fathers, brothers, maternal uncles, wives, sons, friends and elders,
looked at greatly by those wretched ones with eyes full of tears; leaving his own body he goes as wind.
Into a boundless, very terrible darkness covered with gloom, giver of pleasure and pain, hard to traverse for those of sinful deeds,
unbearable and endless, hard to look at, hard to approach, hard to reach, very hard to pass, always hostile to the most sinful —
dragged by those beings, Yama's men, bound with nooses and struck with hammers, they are led along that great road.
Seeing a creature whose life is exhausted at the end of life, the fearsome messengers of Yama come, wishing to lead him.
At the time of going they are mounted on bears, tigers and asses, others on camels, monkeys, scorpions and wolves,
on owls, snakes and cats, others with vultures as vehicles, on hawks and jackals, with sarasa-birds and herons as vehicles,
others with the faces of boars, animals, vetalas and buffaloes, bearing many forms, terrible, terrifying to all beings,
with long testicles, terrible mouths, crooked noses, three eyes, with huge jaws, cheeks and mouths, hanging teeth and lips,
with protruding teeth of distorted shape like sprouts, limbs smeared with flesh and blood, with fearfully projecting fangs,
with mouths like the nether world, flaming tongues, terrifying, with eyes of distorted shape, flaming, tawny, restless,
like cats, owls, fireflies and Indra's cochineal insects, rough, squinting, stiff, with eyes like fire,
greatly adorned with terrible ornaments, bound like serpents, with red and fine limbs, adorned with garlands of skulls,
with black snakes on their necks, terrifying with hissing sounds, with hair like flames of fire, stiff and rough, fearsome,
covered with brown, tawny, restless tawny beards, with very terrible long arms like iron clubs,
some two-armed there, others four-armed, others sixteen-armed, others with ten or twenty arms,
others with innumerable arms, some with a thousand arms, with weapons of distorted shape, blazing, terrible,
with spears, javelins, discuses and other brilliant weapons of various kinds, with nooses, chains and rods, frightening, very mighty,
the very terrible ones come at the end of mortals' lives to seize all creatures, doers of Yama's command.
The body which is to be tormented, born of one's own actions, that is led for this creature to Yama's abode.
Bound with the nooses of death, with chains and adamantine shackles, greatly beaten by angry Yama's servants, he is led,
stumbling, weeping, crying out again and again "Alas father, mother, son", spoiled by his actions.
Struck with sharp spears, sharp heavy hammers, blows of swords and spears, and terrible diamond-rods,
reviled with great roars, with thunderbolts and spears, each one angry and beating him greatly on all sides,
he, bewildered, pained, burning here and there, dragged, the creature is led along the road by the very terrifying ones,
through kusha thorns, anthills, stakes, stones and gravel, through blazing fire, strewn with hundreds of caustic thunderbolts,
burnt by the rays of the heated blazing sun, he is dragged by Yama's messengers, terrifying with jackal-cries.
Dragged by those terrible ones, eaten by hundreds of jackals, the sinner goes on the dreadful road to Yama's abode.
Sometimes afraid, sometimes terrified, sometimes stumbling, sometimes crying in sorrow, he has to go that great road.
Rebuked, agitated, fled, confounded by fear, with trembling bodies those called living beings must go.
On a road strewn with thorns and burning sand, men who gave no gifts must go, burning.
Those who kill living beings must go with foul smell of fat and blood, goat-like bodies, in crowds, strewn with burnt split skins.
Murderers of living beings must go crying, wailing and shrieking without voice, afflicted with pain, and good ones.
Killers of living beings must go, pierced by spears, bhindipalas, swords, tomaras and arrows, by sharp spear-points.
Sinners must go, eaten by dogs, tigers, wolves and herons.
Eaters of meat must go, cut by saw-strokes and pierced on all sides by tips of horns of buffaloes and bulls,
rooted up by boars; the most sinful destroyers of honey must go, eaten in swarms by needles, bees, crows and flies.
One who kills a trusting master, friend or woman — such cunning men must go cut by weapons.
Those who kill creatures and strike the innocent go on Yama's road eaten by Rakshasas.
Those who steal the fine clothing of others' wives
go fleeing naked to Yama's abode as ghosts. Garments, grain, gold, house or field —
the evil-souled most sinful sinners who steal them are beaten with stones, clubs and rods and, wasted,
bleeding much, must go to Yama's abode. Men here who steal a Brahmin's property, fearless of hell,
and strike Brahmins and revile them, the lowest of men, bound to dry wood with ears, eyes and noses cut off,
smeared with pus and blood, beaten by black vultures and jackals and by terrible, fierce, cruel servants,
go crying, sinners, to Yama's abode: such a supremely hard road, blazing with fire.
The Raurava, hard of access and uneven, is indicated for man, the colour of heated copper, with sparks like flames of fire,
strewn with thorns, with wide and terrible beatings, crowded with spears and thunderbolts, brilliant, with sharp thorns,
mixed with live-coal sand, hard to traverse because of fire-insects, filled with garlands of flames, terrible, heated by the sun's rays.
The embodied soul is led on that road, dragged by the very cruel; whenever a creature cries out, fallen somewhere, pained,
then he is struck by all Yama's servants with weapons. Thus beaten, the greedy one who has no policy in sin
is led helpless by the unrestrainable servants of Yama. All must go on that road, very hard to traverse.
He is led with disdain by various terrible messengers of Yama; having led the creature on that dreadful road, Yama's servants
make him enter a terrible city of copper and iron, Brahmins; that city is vast in form, a hundred thousand yojanas long,
declared square, with four gates, auspicious; its golden ramparts are ten thousand yojanas high.
Adorned with sapphires, great sapphires and rubies, that city is terrible, filled with various terrible hosts,
with gods, Danavas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Rakshasas and serpents. Its auspicious east gate is adorned with hundreds of banners,
decorated with diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli and pearls, crowded with song and dance by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
By it the entry is of gods, sages and yogis, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Yakshas, and Vidyadharas moving about.
The north city gate is adorned with bells and chauris, arranged with umbrellas and chauris, decorated with many jewels,
with lovely lute and flute sounds, resounding with auspicious songs, with the sounds of Rik, Yajus and Sama, crowded with groups of sages.
By it enter the knowers of dharma, devoted to truthful vows, and men who gave water in summer and fire in winter,
those who massaged the weary, those fond of speaking kindly, those fond of giving, heroes, those devoted to their mother and father,
those always engaged in serving Brahmins and worshipping guests. The western great gate of the city is adorned with jewels,
with steps of variegated gems, adorned with arches, resounding with bheri and mridanga, conch and kahala.
Always filled with delighted Siddha groups, resounding with auspicious sounds; by it enter the delighted men devoted to Shiva,
those bathed in all holy places, those who served the five fires, heroes who died on departure, died on Mount Kalanjara,
those heroes who perished in fire, who accomplished a fast to death, those killed in a crowded cattle-raid for master, friend or people —
those heroes, rich in austerity, enter by the west, of that city's very terrible one, terrifying to all beings.
The southern gate is of this kind, filled with cries of alas, joined with darkness and sharp horns,
with thorns, scorpions, serpents, diamond-insects, hard to traverse, with plundering wolves, tigers, bears, lions and jackals,
with dogs, cats and vultures, with mouths holding mouthfuls of flames; by it the entry is always of all wrongdoers,
those who kill Brahmins, cows, children, the old and the sick, one come for refuge, one trusting, a woman, a friend, or one unarmed —
